hints: A `std::map` iterates in sorted key order.
exercises.solution: It prints `apple7 fig1 pear3`. A `std::map` is a sorted tree, so iteration visits keys in alphabetical order regardless of insertion order, and the second `m["apple"]` finds the existing entry and adds 2 to it.

hints: `lower_bound` finds the first element not less than 4; `upper_bound` the first element greater than 4.
The distance between them is the number of 4s.
exercises.solution: It prints `1 4 3`. The first element `>= 4` is at index 1; the first element `> 4` is the 7 at index 4. Together they bracket every 4 in the sorted vector, so `hi - lo` counts them: 3. `std::ranges::equal_range` returns both iterators at once.

Not yet — `take(2)` stops after two elements.

hints: Which elements are odd, in order?
Multiply the first two of them by 10.
exercises.solution: The odd elements in order are 3, 1, 9, 7; transformed they are 30, 10, 90, 70; `take(2)` keeps `30 10`. The full output with GCC 14 is `30 10 | 4 calls`: the predicate ran on 3, 8, 1, *and 9*. After yielding the second element, the loop advanced the iterator once more before noticing that `take` was exhausted, and advancing a filter iterator means searching for the next match. That is why predicates in pipelines should not have side effects.

exercises.prompt: In the previous exercise's program, how many times was the predicate `odd` called in total, as printed by GCC 14? (Think about what the range-`for` loop does after it receives the second element.)

Not yet — views are lazy. The pipeline never looks at elements it does not need.

hints: A range-`for` loop increments the iterator and *then* compares it with the end.
Incrementing `take`'s iterator increments the filter iterator underneath, which searches for the next odd element.
exercises.solution: **4**. To produce 30 the filter tested 3; to produce 10 it tested 8 and 1. Then the loop did `++it` before comparing with the end: `take`'s iterator decremented its count to 0 and advanced the underlying filter iterator, which tested 9 (odd, so it stopped there). Only then did the comparison with the end say the loop was finished. Views do the minimum work needed by the iteration protocol, which is close to, but not exactly, the number of elements you consume.

exercises.prompt: A program reads about 200,000 (word, count) updates from a text, looks up words very often, and at the end prints every word **in alphabetical order** once. Which approach is the most sensible starting point?

options.label: Count in a `std::unordered_map`, then copy the entries into a vector and sort it once for printing.
options.feedback: Yes. Hash lookups suit the many updates, and a single O(n log n) sort at the end is cheaper than keeping everything sorted all the time. (A `std::map` is also a reasonable, simpler choice; measure if it matters.)

options.label: A `std::list` of pairs, searched linearly for each word.
options.feedback: Not yet — each lookup would be O(n), making the whole job roughly quadratic, with poor memory locality on top.

options.label: A `std::vector` of pairs, re-sorted after every update.
options.feedback: Not yet — sorting 200,000 times costs far more than sorting once.

options.label: A `std::priority_queue` of pairs.
options.feedback: Not yet — a priority queue only gives fast access to its largest element; it cannot look up a word.

hints: Separate the two phases: many lookups, then one ordered print.
Which container is fastest at lookups when order does not matter during the counting?
exercises.solution: Use a hash map for the counting phase, where lookups dominate and order is irrelevant, then sort once at the end. A `std::map` gives ordered output for free and is perfectly reasonable too; it pays O(log n) per lookup instead. The list and repeatedly sorted vector have the wrong complexity, and a priority queue does not support lookup at all.

exercises.prompt: `std::vector<int> v` holds 4 elements and has capacity 4. `int* p = &v[1];` Which of the following operations may leave `p` dangling? Select all that apply.

options.label: `v.push_back(5);`
options.feedback: Yes. The vector is full, so it must reallocate and move every element to new memory.

options.label: `v[3] = 10;`
options.feedback: Not yet — assigning to an element changes a value in place; nothing moves.

options.label: `v.erase(v.begin());`
options.feedback: Yes. Erasing shifts every later element one place left; `p` now points at what used to be `v[2]` (and iterators after the erase point are invalid).

options.label: `std::ranges::sort(v);`
options.feedback: Not yet — sorting swaps values around inside the same memory. `p` still points at `v[1]`, though the value there may have changed.

hints: Ask whether each operation can move elements to new memory or shift them to new positions.
exercises.solution: (a) reallocates because the vector is at capacity, invalidating every pointer, reference and iterator. (c) shifts later elements down, so `p` no longer refers to the element it used to. (b) and (d) keep every element in the same storage; with (d) the *value* at `p` may change, but `p` is still valid.
